00At a glance

Four different layers of the stack: two are weights you add, one is a second model in the same run, one is a sampling-time trick.

FeatureWhere you touch itWhat it actually doesCostState here
Textual Inversion Train tab → Create embedding / Train; then a word in the prompt Adds new vectors to CLIP's token table — a word the model learns to understand ~3 KB per vector, free at inference no embeddings
Hypernetworks Train tab → Create hypernetwork; then <hypernet:name:1.0> Small MLPs that nudge cross-attention K/V at every step +compute every attention layer empty folder
Refiner Refiner accordion in txt2img and img2img Swaps to a second UNet for the last ~20% of the sampling steps one model reload mid-generation needs a refiner ckpt
Soft inpainting img2img → Soft inpainting accordion Blends original ↔ generated latents every step by mask opacity, then composites by measured change a little extra Python per step builtin, active
Want a new word?

Textual Inversion. Cheapest possible way to teach "my character", "this art style", or a reusable negative like "watermark" — a few kilobytes, no checkpoint surgery.

Want a style overlay?

Hypernetwork … but reach for a LoRA first. The LoRA extension is installed here; hypernetworks are the older, slower branch of the same idea.

Want finer SDXL output?

Refiner. Both checkpoints in this fork are SDXL, so this is the one feature that is one download away from working properly.

01Textual Inversion

Teaching CLIP a new word. The model's weights never change — you add rows to its token-embedding table and train only those rows.

What's actually happening

A prompt becomes 77 token slots. Each token is looked up in CLIP's embedding matrix (768 numbers wide for SD 1.5's ViT-L). Textual Inversion adds a new entry to that table: one or more 768-d vectors that get spliced into the token sequence wherever your chosen word appears.

Training freezes the UNet and the text encoder and only moves those few vectors: the model reconstructs your dataset images from captions that contain the new word, and the gradient lands exclusively on your vector. That's why the result is kilobytes instead of gigabytes.

The 30-second version

1 · create
name it, pick how many vectors
→
2 · train
1:1 images + .txt captions
→
3 · use
the name is now a prompt word

No extra VRAM at inference, no model swap, and it stacks with LoRA and with the checkpoint you already use.

What a finished embedding looks like

How to try it

  1. Gather 10–40 images of one thing — one face, one style, one object — as 1:1 ratio crops, each with a .txt caption containing a placeholder word you will later rename (e.g. sks style). The training tab insists on 1:1.
  2. Create the embedding with 1 vector per token unless the concept is complex; then use Number of vectors per token 2–8.
  3. Train with learning rate 0.005, batch 1, and watch the preview images every ~500 steps. Stop when the preview stops improving — the step counter is in the preview strip.
  4. Use it by typing the name where you'd type a word: photo of my_style castle, or weight it: (my_style:1.2). In the negative prompt the same syntax gives you reusable "no watermark" tokens.
How activation really works here

There is no <embedding:…> tag in this fork — the tokenizer matches the embedding's name tokens inside the prompt (EmbeddingDatabase.find_embedding_at_position, modules/textual_inversion/textual_inversion.py:245). That's why the Extra Networks card inserts plain text and why classic prompt weighting (name:1.2) is what you use to dial strength.

Gotchas

  • 77-token budget. The prompt window is fixed at 77 tokens (75 usable). An 8-vector embedding eats 8 of them; a 75-vector one eats the whole window.
  • Architecture-specific. The vectors are text-encoder dimensions; an SD 1.5 embedding is not meaningful on the SDXL checkpoints installed here. Train on the family you'll generate with.
  • Training needs the whole model in VRAM. Both training paths assert against --lowvram.
  • It's a vocabulary patch, not a new ability. TI is great for styles, faces, objects and negatives; it's poor at teaching composition or a concept the model has zero grounding for. That's what LoRA is for.
  • Hashes. textual_inversion_add_hashes_to_infotext is on by default, so PNG info will pin the exact embedding version that made an image.

02Hypernetworks

A small network bolted onto the cross-attention of a frozen model. Same spirit as LoRA, different insertion point, much older lineage.

What's actually happening

For each text-conditioning width you enable, a hypernetwork holds two tiny MLPs — one for the K projection and one for the V projection of every cross-attention layer. Each one is a residual: 

# modules/hypernetworks/hypernetwork.py:118
def forward(self, x):
    return x + self.linear(x) * (self.multiplier if not self.training else 1)

So at multiplier 1.0 you add a learned offset to the attention keys/values; at 0.0 the hypernetwork disables itself; above 1.0 you amplify it. The base model never changes — which is why one file can style many checkpoints, and why it costs compute on every step.

Layer structure

The 1, 2, 1 default means: input width → twice as wide hidden layer → back to input width. It must start and end with 1 because it has to be addable to the original tensor. 1, 2, 2, 1 gives you a deeper adapter.

Create hypernetwork · defaults in this forkmodules/ui.py:1161

Be honest about the trade-off

Hypernetworks were the pre-LoRA answer to "make a style stick". They add a matmul per attention layer at every step (slower than LoRA), they're trained per base model, and quality plateaus earlier. With the builtin LoRA extension already present in this fork, treat hypernetworks as an experiment rather than a workflow — pick it when you specifically want a soft, global nudge and don't mind the speed hit.

How to try it

  1. Create with only the widths you need — for SDXL-class models start with the default set; for SD 1.5 the 768 module alone is enough.
  2. Train with the same 1:1 dataset shape as Textual Inversion; the shared Train tab drives both. Keep the learning rate tiny (1e-5 default) — it's easy to overshoot into mush.
  3. Compare at 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.5 multipliers on the same seed. Above ~1.5 you usually start seeing blown highlights and repeated textures; the multiplier is a dial, not a switch.

Gotchas

  • Training refuses to run under --lowvram, same as embeddings.
  • The activation dropdown excludes hardswish and multiheadattention on purpose (modules/hypernetworks/ui.py:5).
  • Multiplier 0 is a clean kill switch — useful for A/B testing without unloading the file.
  • Two modules per width (K and V) means the file grows with every width you tick, and so does the per-step cost.

03Refiner

The only feature here that changes the model mid-run: sample the composition with the base model, then finish with a second UNet.

What's actually happening

SDXL ships as two models: a base that builds structure, and a refiner that was trained on the last, lowest-noise steps. The Refiner accordion keeps the same latent and, at your chosen point, reloads weights from the second checkpoint and keeps sampling.

A1111 evaluates the switch point in apply_refiner() (modules/sd_samplers_common.py:158). By default that's the model timestep ratio; the setting “Switch to refiner by sampling steps instead of model timesteps” switches to plain step / total_steps — the old behaviour, handy when you change step counts or samplers and want the split to stay put.

There is no refiner checkpoint installed

models/Stable-diffusion/ currently holds CyberRealisticPony_V17.0_FP16 and novaAnimeXL_ilV180 — both are base-style SDXL checkpoints, not refiners. The dropdown will look empty-ish and picking another base model as a "refiner" just re-runs the same architecture on the tail. Pull the official refiner through the Hugging Face mirror this project requires: 

# PowerShell — HF mirror, never huggingface.co directly
$env:HF_ENDPOINT = "https://hf-mirror.com"
huggingface-cli download stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-refiner-1.0 `
  --include "sd_xl_refiner_1.0.safetensors" `
  --local-dir models/Stable-diffusion `
  --endpoint https://hf-mirror.com

How to try it

  1. Download the refiner as above, hit the ↻ next to the Checkpoint dropdown, and pick it.
  2. Run a 30-step comparison on one fixed seed: refiner off, then Switch at 0.8, then 0.6. Look at faces, text, fine texture — the tail steps own those.
  3. If you use hires fix, check Settings → Hires fix: which pass to enable refiner for; the default second pass means the base pass runs alone.

Gotchas

  • The accordion appears in both txt2img and img2img; the pipeline is identical.
  • Refiner checkpoints are tied to the base family. Mixing an SD 1.5 model as "refiner" under an SDXL base produces noise, not polish.
  • Switch at 1.0 silently disables the swap without unticking the box — a common "why is nothing happening".
  • Every swap re-uploads weights; batched runs pay it per image, so it's a quality/speed decision, not a free win.

04Soft inpainting

Inpainting where the mask edge is a gradient, not a cut. The original image fights the denoiser at every step, weighted by the mask.

What's actually happening

Normal inpainting blends once, at the end. Soft inpainting blends inside the sampling loop: at every step the current latent is interpolated back toward the original latent, with the mask (raised to a sigma-dependent power) deciding who wins. 

# extensions-builtin/soft-inpainting
t = nmask ** ((sigma ** schedule_bias) * preservation_strength)
latent = init * (1 - t) + current * t   # + magnitude fix-up

Because sigma shrinks as sampling proceeds, the same mask means something different early and late — that's the whole trick, and the reason a feathered brush stroke actually stays soft.

After sampling, a second pass measures how much each pixel's latent changed and keeps the original pixels wherever the change was small. So the feature is two mechanisms: a per-step latent blend, and a change-aware pixel composite.

How to try it

  1. Use a real image from outputs/img2img-images; paint with a soft brush or drop the mask blur up. The extension's own help text says: “High Mask blur values are recommended!”
  2. Change something subtle — jacket colour, lighting direction, expression — with denoising 0.35–0.6. Hard-edged inpainting fights you here; soft inpainting is built for exactly this.
  3. Tune the seam first, not the content. If the edge is visible: raise Preservation strength or Mask blur. If detail washes out: raise Transition contrast boost. If the edit barely applies: lower Difference threshold.
  4. Prompt the whole image, not just the patch. The model is still denoising a full-frame latent.

Gotchas

  • img2img only. show() returns AlwaysVisible for img2img and False for txt2img.
  • A mask must exist. Without image_mask/mask/nmask the whole feature no-ops.
  • It turns off mask rounding on purpose (p.mask_round = False) — don't be surprised by softer mask edges.
  • Ghosting is a feature. Regions the denoiser barely changed keep the original pixels; with very low denoising the result can look like the edit was ignored.
  • Six numbers in infotext. All of them are recorded, so paste-back restores the exact blend.

3Embedding for a recurring subject 20 crops, captions with a placeholder word, 1 vector, lr 0.005 Whether the word alone reproduces the subject at checkpoint-level quality ~30 min
4Hypernetwork as a style nudge Default widths, 1,2,1, swish, lr 1e-5 Multiplier sweep 0 / 0.5 / 1 / 1.5; compare against an equivalent LoRA ~1 h
Front-end parity note

All four are Gradio/PC features. The fork's mobile front-end (mobile_lite/, served at /mlite/) exposes Text and Image (img2img + inpaint) only — it has no refiner, no soft-inpainting, no hypernetwork or embedding pickers, and the builtin mobile extension is a layout tweak only. So there is nothing to mirror on the mobile side unless you want a new feature there.

06API cheat sheet

Same features, no clicking. Run against your own instance on 127.0.0.1:7860.

Refiner — plain request fields

refiner_checkpoint and refiner_switch_at are real columns on the processing dataclass (modules/processing.py:186), so they're part of the request schema. The accordion's setup() — which would clear them — is skipped for API calls (ScriptBuiltinUI.setup_for_ui_only), so setting the fields is enough: 

POST /sdapi/v1/txt2img
{
  "prompt": "portrait of an astronaut, cinematic",
  "steps": 30,
  "refiner_checkpoint": "sd_xl_refiner_1.0.safetensors [31e35c80fc]",
  "refiner_switch_at": 0.8
}

Soft inpainting — always-on script

Always-on scripts are addressed by title().lower() (modules/api/api.py:35), so the key is literally "soft inpainting". Args are positional, in UI order: 

POST /sdapi/v1/img2img
{
  "init_images": ["<base64>"],
  "mask": "<base64 grayscale>",
  "denoising_strength": 0.45,
  "mask_blur": 12,
  "alwayson_scripts": {
    "soft inpainting": {
      "args": [true, 1.0, 0.5, 4.0, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0]
    }
  }
}

order: enabled, schedule bias, preservation strength, transition contrast boost, mask influence, difference threshold, difference contrast — the defaults.

Embeddings & hypernetworks — prompt text only

There is no API object for these: they are activated by the prompt string (embedding name as a word, or <hypernet:name:0.8>). List what's loaded with GET /sdapi/v1/embeddings, and remember that a new file only appears after a refresh/model load.
